title.en: Pangu Opens Heaven and Earth: The Cosmogony of the Primal Giant

region.en: Nanyang, Henan (Pangu Mountain shrine; symbolic pin)
region.zh: 中國河南盤古山（象徵性定位）

texts.period: First recorded by Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (3rd c. CE; text lost, fragments preserved in Yiwen Leiju, 7th c.); cult attested Tang-Song onward

source.archive: Internet Sacred Texts Archive (Werner, Myths and Legends of China, 1922) / Project Gutenberg
source.work: Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (fragments in Yiwen Leiju); trans. Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction (Baltimore, 1993); E. T. C. Werner, Myths and Legends of China, London 1922

texts.license: Werner 1922 public domain; Birrell 1993 quoted only as summary (copyright) — passages are labeled paraphrases

summary.en: Heaven and earth begin as an egg-like chaos in which the giant Pangu grows for eighteen thousand years; when he wakes he splits the light and heavy, and each day the sky rises ten feet and the earth thickens ten feet while he stands between them; at his death his body becomes the world — breath the winds, eyes the sun and moon, blood the rivers — and the mites on his flesh become the peoples.
summary.zh: 太初如雞卵之混沌，盤古生其中，萬八千歲而醒；陽清為天，陰濁為地，天日高一丈，地日厚一丈，盤古居中長成；其死也，氣為風雲，聲為雷霆，左眼為日，右眼為月，血液為江河，肢為五嶽——身上諸蟲受風所感化為黎民。

sensitivity.note: Heritage narrative; living folk cult at Pangu shrines treats it as sacred geography.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (as preserved in fragments): Heaven and earth were together like the inside of an egg; Pangu was born within; after eighteen thousand years the clear and light rose to become heaven, the heavy and turbid settled to become earth, and Pangu stood between, growing ten feet a day as heaven rose and earth thickened ten feet a day — for another eighteen thousand years. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Xu Zheng, Sanwu liji (as preserved in fragments); not verbatim.

passages.text: Condensed paraphrase of the death catalogue (Sanwu liji fragments): At his death, his breath became the winds and clouds, his voice the thunder, his left eye the sun and right eye the moon, his four limbs and body the four poles and five mountains, his blood the rivers, his veins the roads, his flesh the fields, his hair and beard the stars, his skin and body-hair plants and trees, his teeth and bones metals and stones, his marrow pearls and jade, his sweat the rain — and the mites on his body, touched by the wind, became the black-haired people. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of the death catalogue (Sanwu liji fragments); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Johns Hopkins, 1993 (copyright); E. T. C. Werner, Myths and Legends of China, 1922 (public domain)

narrative.en:
Pangu is China's best-known cosmogonic figure, though a latecomer to the textual record: the story first appears in a 3rd-century CE encyclopedia, at a time when Daoist cosmology and Indian Buddhist creation stories circulated at court, and it became the dominant folk cosmogony of imperial and modern China.

BEGINNING: THE EGG OF CHAOS. Heaven and earth were once joined without shape or boundary, undifferentiated like the inside of a hen's egg (hundun, the primal murk). Within this chaos the primal being Pangu was born and grew — asleep for eighteen thousand years in the dark. When he woke, he could not endure the confinement; he took up a chisel and mallet (or, in other tellings, stretched his limbs) and split the chaos: the clear, light qi rose and became heaven; the heavy, turbid qi sank and became earth.

MIDDLE: THE STANDING GIANT. Fearing that heaven and earth would close again, Pangu stood between them, his head holding up the sky, his feet planted on the earth — and he grew with them: each day heaven rose ten feet, the earth thickened ten feet, and Pangu grew ten feet taller, for another eighteen thousand years, until the poles were fixed at their proper distance and the giant had become taller than any being could measure.

END: THE DEATH THAT IS THE WORLD. Exhausted, Pangu died — and his death is the creation's second act: his last breath became the winds and clouds; his voice, the rolling thunder; his left eye the sun, his right eye the moon; his four limbs and trunk became the four poles and the Five Mountains; his blood the rivers, his veins the roads of the land, his flesh the fields and soil; his hair and beard the stars of heaven, his skin and body-hair the grasses and trees; his teeth and bones metals and rocks, his marrow pearls and jade, his sweat the rain and dew that nourishes all. The mites and lice that lived on his flesh, touched by the wind, became the black-haired people — human beings born not from a god's design but from the body of the one who made the world possible.

AFTERMATH AND FUNCTION. The Sanwu liji continues with the Three Sovereigns who follow Pangu (Heaven, Earth, Man), grounding dynastic succession in cosmic succession; Pangu's cult centers (Pangu Mountain in Henan; shrines across the south; the Yao and Zhuang Pangu traditions of Guangdong/Guangxi) treat him as local ancestor. The myth's functions: it aitiologizes topography (mountains as limbs, rivers as blood — a body-map of China), establishes the cosmos as organism rather than artifact, and, in the modern era, became the centerpiece of Chinese national myth-history (Pangu statues, the Pangu Era of textbooks).

COMPARATIVE NOTE. Scholars have long compared Pangu to the dismembered-cosmos figures of other traditions (Ymir in Norse myth; Purusha in the Rigveda's Purusha Sukta; Manu in Indo-Iranian texts) and debated South Asian influence on the 3rd-century story (the giant from the cosmic egg), while Chinese folk tradition holds him indigenous. The record keeps both positions open.
narrative.zh: 盤古之名首見於三國吳徐整《三五曆紀》，其時佛教創世說與道教宇宙論並行，而盤古遂為後世民間創世之主。太初天地混沌如雞子，盤古生其中，萬八千歲；覺而惡其困，執鑿開混沌：陽清為天，陰濁為地；恐復合，以身居中，頭托天、足踏地，天日高一丈、地日厚一丈、盤古日長一丈，又一萬八千歲，天地極深而極固。後盤古力竭而死：氣成風雲，聲為雷霆，左眼為日右眼為月，四肢五體為四極五嶽，血液為江河，筋脈為地理，肌肉為田土，髮髭為星辰，皮毛為草木，齒骨為金石，精髓為珠玉，汗流為雨澤；身上諸蟲感風化為黎民——人非神所設計，乃開天者之身所遺。續以三皇承之，王朝承宇宙之序。功能：地形之釋義（山為肢、河為血——中國之地圖即身體圖）、宇宙為有機體、及現代民族神話之核心（盤古紀元）。比較：與北歐尤彌爾、吠陀原人普魯沙結構平行，學界有印度影響說，民間則自認本土。

functions: Topographical aition: mountains as limbs, rivers as blood — the body-map of the land
Cosmos as organism: creation as growth and death rather than craft
Succession template: the Three Sovereigns and dynastic order follow cosmic order
Modern national myth-history: Pangu statues and the 'Pangu Era' of textbooks

variants.name: Xu Zheng's Sanwu liji (3rd c. CE)
variants.text_tradition: Text lost; fragments preserved in the Yiwen Leiju encyclopedia (7th c.) and Taiping Yulan
variants.summary: The earliest telling: the egg-chaos, the eighteen-thousand-year growth, the ten-foot-a-day measure, and the full death-catalogue; no chisel — Pangu splits chaos by growing.

variants.name: Wu Yueneng? 'Pangu Kai Tiandi' folk versions (Henan/Shandong)
variants.text_tradition: 20th-c. oral recordings at Pangu Mountain (Nanyang) and folk storytellers
variants.summary: Folk tellings add the chisel-and-mallet, the sister-spouse motif (Pangu and his sister repopulate the world, with smoke-sign divination), and local shrine genealogies — the living folk stratum.

variants.name: South Asian parallel (Purusha/Manu hypothesis)
variants.summary: The dismembered-cosmos structure parallels the Vedic Purusha, and the cosmic egg parallels Brahmanda; scholars debate transmission via Buddhist India in the Han-Song interval versus independent development.

variants.name: Pangu in Yao and Zhuang traditions
variants.text_tradition: Guangdong/Guangxi minority narratives; Pan Hu figure
variants.summary: Southern minority traditions entwine Pangu with Pan Hu (the dog-ancestor of the Yao), a distinct but etymologically tangled figure — caution against conflating them is standard in scholarship.

primary_sources.citation: 3rd c. CE; fragments in Ouyang Xun (ed.), Yiwen Leiju, ch. 1 (7th c.) and Taiping Yulan; English in Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction, Baltimore 1993, pp. 25-28 (copyright; quoted as summary only).

secondary_sources.work: Anne Birrell, Chinese Mythology: An Introduction
secondary_sources.citation: Birrell 1993, Baltimore: Johns Hopkins University Press — annotated translations and the dating debate.
Bodde 1961, in Mythologies of the Ancient World (ed. S. N. Kramer), New York: Doubleday — the South Asian influence argument.

title.en: Izanagi and Izanami: The Stirring of the Islands and the Land of Yomi
title.zh: 伊邪那岐與伊邪那美：淤能碁呂島與黃泉國

region.en: Onogoro Island / Awaji, Seto Inland Sea (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 瀨戶內海淤能碁呂島／淡路島（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Kojiki compiled 712 CE (principal MS: Shinpukuji-bon, 1371 copy); Nihon Shoki 720 CE

source.work: Kojiki, Book 1, trans. Basil Hall Chamberlain, A Translation of the 'Ko-ji-ki', Kobe, 1882 (public domain)

summary.en: The divine pair Izanagi and Izanami stir the primordial brine with the jeweled spear to raise Onogoro island, marry with a circuit of the celestial pillar, and beget the islands of Japan and the gods; when Izanami dies bearing the fire-god, Izanagi follows her to Yomi, breaks the taboo of looking, flees her putrefying corpse, seals the land of the dead with a boulder, and purifies himself — begetting Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susanoo.
summary.zh: 伊邪那岐與伊邪那美以天沼矛攪滄海，滴鹹成淤能碁呂島；繞天柱成婚，生大八洲與諸神；火神焚母而死，伊邪那岐赴黃泉，破『勿視』之禁，見腐屍而逃，以大石封黃泉比良坂，於日向橘小戶之阿波岐原祓禊，遂生天照、月讀、須佐之男。

sensitivity.note: Living Shinto tradition; the imperial mythology's modern political history (State Shinto, 1868-1945) should be handled critically.

passages.text: Chamberlain translation (Kojiki 1.3): 'So the two Deities, standing on the Floating Bridge of Heaven, pushed down the jewel-spear with a churning-churning, and lingered? and when they had churned the brine till it went curdle-curdle, and drew [the spear] up, the brine that dripped down from the end of the spear was piled up and became an island. This is the island of Onogoro.' (Close to Chamberlain's wording; quoted as public-domain translation.)

Condensed paraphrase of Kojiki 1.8-9 (Chamberlain, public domain source): At Yomi's gate Izanagi breaks the tooth of his left comb and lights it; he sees his wife's body crawling with maggots and the eight thunder-deities on it; fleeing, he casts his headdress (grapes), his comb (bamboo shoots), and peaches to delay the pursuit; at the pass he plugs it with a boulder of a thousand men — and the pair exchange threats: she will strangle a thousand a day, he will build fifteen hundred birthing-huts. Not verbatim.
passages.note: Condensed paraphrase of Kojiki 1.8-9 (Chamberlain, public domain source); not verbatim.

texts.canonical_translation: Basil Hall Chamberlain, A Translation of the 'Ko-ji-ki', Kobe 1882 (public domain); W. G. Aston, Nihongi, 1896 (public domain); modern: Donald Philippi, Kojiki, Tokyo 1968 (copyright)

narrative.en:
The Kojiki (712 CE) opens the age of gods with the first stirrings of creation and the first death — a narrative whose movements structure Shinto purity practice to this day.

BEGINNING: THE STIRRING. When heaven and earth first parted, three gods came into being, and the seven generations of the age of gods followed; the last pair, Izanagi ('He Who Invites') and Izanami ('She Who Invites'), stand on the Floating Bridge of Heaven with the jeweled spear Ame-no-nuboko. They churn the sea beneath ('churning-churning'); lifting the spear, the brine drips from its point and piles into the island Onogoro. Descending, they erect the Heavenly Pillar (Ame-no-mihashira) and circle it in the marriage rite: she greets him first — 'how lovely a young man!' — and he answers her greeting. The children of this first union are deformed: the leech-child Hiruko, set adrift in a reed boat, and Awashima. They return and ask the Heavenly Deities the cause; the gods divine it — the woman spoke first. They repeat the rite with the man first, and the union is made right.

MIDDLE: THE BIRTH OF THE ISLANDS AND OF DEATH. Izanami now bears the islands of Japan — Awaji, Shikoku, Oki, Kyushu, Iki, Tsushima, Sado, and Yamato ('the fairest land') — and then the gods of sea, wind, mountains, trees, and plains. Last she bears the fire-god Kagutsuchi; his flames burn her genitals, and she sickens — her vomit, excrement, and urine each begetting gods — and she dies. Izanagi, raging, cuts Kagutsuchi in pieces with his ten-grasp sword, and from the blood and the severed parts spring gods (including Takemikazuchi). Grieving, Izanagi follows his wife to Yomi, the land of roots and darkness.

THE TABOO AND THE FLIGHT. Izanami greets him: 'Why hast thou come?... I have eaten of the hearth of Yomi' — too late to return. She retires to consult the gods of the land, forbidding him to look; Izanagi waits, then breaks a tooth from his comb and lights it — and sees the horror: her body crawling with maggots, the eight Thunder-deities lodged on it. He flees; Izanami's shame turns to fury: 'Thou hast brought shame on me!' She sends the hags of Yomi (yomotsu-shikome), then the eight thunder-gods and the warriors of Yomi. Izanagi delays them by casting his black headdress (which becomes grapes), his comb (bamboo shoots), and plucking three peaches to strike at the pursuers — the peaches he names saviors of humanity. At the foot of the Even Pass of Yomi (Yomotsu-hirasaka), he plucks three peaches from a tree and hurls them; the pursuers fall back, and the pass he blocks with a boulder that would take a thousand men to move. From either side of the rock the couple speaks their last: Izanami threatens to strangle a thousand people of his land each day; Izanagi answers he will have fifteen hundred birthing-huts built each day — death and birth locked in ratio. She is proclaimed Yomotsu-Ookami, the great goddess of the dead.

END: THE PURIFICATION AND THE THREE NOBLE CHILDREN. Pollution-clad, Izanagi performs the first great purification (misogi) at Awajihara (Tachibana no Odo) in Himuka: casting his clothes and staff into the water begets gods of each garment; washing his left eye begets Amaterasu-Omikami (Heaven-Illuminating Great Deity), his right eye Tsukuyomi (Moon), his nose Susanoo (Storm). 'Rejoicing, he divides his treasures': Amaterasu receives the High Plain of Heaven with the necklace, Tsukuyomi the night, Susanoo the seas — and Susanoo wails for his mother until his beard reaches his chest, laying waste to the lands. Izanagi expels him — and the next cycle begins. The narrative grounds Shinto purity (kegara? kegare and harae): death is pollution, water purification, and the sun's lineage the world's light.
narrative.zh: 天地下分之初，神世七代之末生伊邪那岐、伊邪那美二神。二神立於天浮橋，以天沼矛攪滄海，提起時矛尖滴鹹積為淤能碁呂島；下島立天之御柱，繞柱成婚：妹先言『好男子』，遂生水蛭子，棄於蘆舟；歸問天神，知女先言之故；男先言，復生大八洲（淡路、四國、隱岐、九州、壹岐、對馬、佐渡、大和）與海山風木諸神。末生火神迦具土，焚母陰而病，吐泄亦化神，遂死。伊邪那岐怒斬火神為五段，血與斷部化神。悲而赴黃泉；伊邪那美言已食黃泉灶火之食，不得歸，囑勿視；伊邪那岐折左鬢櫛齒燃火照之，見屍蛆蠕、八雷神附，驚逃。妻怒曰『辱我』，遣黃泉醜女、八雷神、黃泉軍追之；丟鬢飾化葡萄、櫛化筍、擲桃退敵；至黃泉比良坂取桃三枚投之，以千人所引大石塞坂。隔石互誓：妻日殺千人，夫日立千五百產室——生死相抵。妻為黃泉大神。穢甚，遂於日向橘小戶阿波岐原祓禊：濯左眼生天照大御神、右眼生月讀、鼻生須佐之男，分寶而命之；須佐之男啼欲見母，毀山川，被逐——次一神話由此而始。功能：穢與祓之禮、死為穢之釋義、日光之世系。

functions: Grounding of Shinto purity practice: kegare (pollution) and harae (purification)
Aition of death as pollution and of the birth/death ratio in the world
Charter of the solar lineage: Amaterasu's birth from the left eye
Political theology: the imperial genealogy descends from this cosmogony

variants.name: Nihon Shoki version (720 CE)
variants.text_tradition: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, trans. W. G. Aston, 1896 (public domain)
variants.summary: The official chronicle's parallel telling with multiple textual variants appended (itself quoting 'one writing' versions), softer in tone (no maggot catalogue) and ordered for courtly legitimation.

variants.name: Kojiki's Shinpukuji-bon manuscript
variants.summary: The oldest surviving full manuscript of the 712 text, the base of modern critical editions; earlier Kojiki quotations survive in the Kokki? and Kogo Shui (807).

variants.name: Local Yomi traditions
variants.text_tradition: Yomotsu-hirasaka (Higashiizumo, Shimane) shrine traditions; Yomi cult sites
variants.summary: The Even Pass of Yomi is localized in Shimane prefecture, where the boulder (chigaeshi-no-oka) is a cult site — the myth as sacred geography maintained by living shrines.

primary_sources.citation: Chs. 1.3-1.9 (stirring, marriage, births, fire-god, Yomi, purification). MS: Shinpukuji-bon (1371 copy). Translations: B. H. Chamberlain, Kobe 1882 (public domain); D. Philippi, Tokyo 1968 (copyright).

secondary_sources.work: Gary L. Ebersole, Ritual Poetry and the Politics of Death in Early Japan
secondary_sources.citation: Ebersole 1989, Princeton: Princeton University Press — the Yomi narrative's ritual and political poetics.

secondary_sources.work: Michael Ashkenazi, Handbook of Japanese Mythology
secondary_sources.citation: Ashkenazi 2003, Santa Barbara: ABC-CLIO — reference synthesis of Kojiki/Nihongi variants.

texts.sensitivity_guidance: Living Shinto tradition and imperial mythology: cite Kojiki by chapter; handle the 1868-1945 State Shinto use of this material critically in commentary; shrine sites in Shimane maintain active cults of the Yomi narrative.
